title: Water Cost Exposure Score
subtitle: Scores how exposed your planned hotel, senior living or multifamily building is to 20 years of rising water and sewer rates, across rate assumptions, fixture choices, metering and reuse readiness, and

questions.text: What is the projected year-one water and sewer bill for this building?
questions.hint: Use the utility estimate or your MEP engineer's demand model. For scale, a hotel uses about 209 gallons per occupied room per day and senior living about 109 gallons per resident per day. Enter 0 if nobody has estimated it yet.

questions.text: What annual water and sewer rate increase does your proforma assume?
questions.hint: Enter 0 if the model holds water and sewer flat. The scoring gives 10 points per percentage point, so 10% or higher scores full marks, the top of the 4% to 10% range I use in 20-year projections.

questions.text: What is the highest annual water and sewer increase your utility has approved or proposed for the next five years?
questions.hint: Check the council or utility rate study and round to the nearest whole percent. Recent examples are Denver at about 5.5%, Charlotte about 6.5% for multifamily, Phoenix up to 13% and St. Louis proposing up to 18%. The scoring subtracts 10 points per percentage point, so a market at 10% or higher scores 0.

questions.text: How was the water and sewer escalation rate in your proforma chosen?

answers.label: It copies the general inflation line, or water is held flat
Someone picked a round number like 3% and nobody has questioned it
We used the utility's published increase for next year only
We used the utility's multi-year rate plan and ran a higher case
We modelled 4%, 6%, 8% and 10% over 20 years and the deal holds at the high case

questions.text: At 8% a year, the water and sewer bill at year 20 is 4.66 times today's. What happens to this building's NOI when you run that number?

answers.label: Nobody has run it
We ran it and left it out of the investor model
We know NOI takes a hit, and the design has not changed because of it
The number is in the model and it moved at least one design decision
The 8% case is our base underwriting case, and the design reduces potable demand to cover it

low.headline: Your proforma has a flat water line on a rising bill
low.text: When I run 20-year ROI projections I used to use 4% a year, and I now think that is too low for a lot of markets. At 4% the bill is 2.19 times today's by year 20. At 8% it is 4.66 times. If your model holds water flat, the gap starts compounding in year one and you will see it in NOI around year eight.
steps: Pull your utility's published multi-year rate plan
Rerun the proforma at 4%, 6%, 8% and 10% water and sewer increases
Put the 20-year difference in front of the investment committee

mid.headline: You have a rate assumption. Test it against your market.
mid.text: You have a number in the model, which puts you ahead of a flat-rate proforma. Now check it against what your utility has published. At a $100,000 year-one bill, the 20-year total is about $2.98M at 4% and about $3.68M at 6%. Two points of difference is roughly $700,000 you did not budget for.
steps: Replace the round-number assumption with the utility's published rate plan
Model a high case at 8% and check whether NOI still meets the investor target
Share the high case with your MEP engineer before plumbing design

high.headline: Your rate assumptions would hold up to a lender's questions
high.text: You modelled real escalation and the deal holds at the high case. The next step is using that number to pay for design decisions. Every gallon of potable demand you remove now is a gallon you never pay the year-20 rate on.
steps: Convert the high-case water cost into a budget for reuse and fixtures
Update the rate study every year during development
Show investors the NOI difference between the base design and a reuse design

questions.text: Where does the water for toilet flushing come from in the current design?

answers.label: Potable water, standard fixtures, and nobody has asked the question
Potable water with low-flow fixtures, and that is the whole water strategy
Potable water for now, with space set aside for a future non-potable riser
Dual plumbing is drawn so toilets can run on recycled water
Toilets are designed to run on treated greywater or harvested rainwater from day one

questions.text: Do you know how the building's demand splits across showers and sinks, toilets, laundry, irrigation and cooling towers?

answers.label: We only have one total demand number from the utility estimate
We know the total and a rough per-unit or per-room figure
MEP has an end-use breakdown, and the development team has not seen it
We have the split and know how much of the demand does not need to be drinking water
We have the split, the greywater supply volume and the non-potable demand it can cover

questions.text: How were the fixtures in this building selected?

answers.label: On unit price in the budget line
To meet the plumbing code minimum
To hit a LEED or green building water-efficiency target
Low-flow fixtures, with the flow rates fed into a 20-year water cost model
Fixtures and the reuse system were sized together, so each saving is counted once and the payback is known

low.headline: Your toilets flush drinking water you pay for twice
low.text: A low-flow toilet still uses 1.6 gallons per flush. You pay to bring that water in as drinking water, and you pay sewer charges to send it back out. In a hotel or senior living building a large share of daily demand does not need to be potable at all, and right now you have no way to see which share.
steps: Ask your MEP engineer for an end-use water breakdown
Mark toilets, irrigation, laundry and cooling towers as non-potable candidates
Reserve space for a non-potable riser before the design is locked

mid.headline: You know the demand. Now separate what needs to be potable.
mid.text: Efficient fixtures lower the bill, and they are the first step. The bigger number is the water that goes down the shower drain and could come back to flush a toilet. For a 200-room hotel, up to 60% of water demand can be recycled.
steps: Size the greywater supply from showers, baths and laundry
Match that supply against toilet and irrigation demand
Draw dual plumbing into the current design set

high.headline: Your fixtures and reuse are designed as one system
high.text: You know where the water goes and you designed for it. The last check is that fixture savings and reuse savings are each counted correctly in the 20-year model, so the payback you show investors is the payback you get.
steps: Run fixture and reuse savings together in one model
Confirm cooling tower make-up water as a reuse candidate
Document the end-use split for the operator

questions.text: How is water metered in the design?

answers.label: One building meter, and the first real data will be the first utility bill
One building meter plus separate irrigation metering
Submeters on major end uses such as laundry, kitchen or cooling towers
Submetering by unit or wing, with the data going to the operator
Submetering by end use and by source, so potable, recycled and rainwater volumes each show up in the monthly report

questions.text: After opening, how would you find out that water and sewer costs are running above the proforma?

answers.label: When the asset manager asks why NOI is down, probably years in
At the annual budget review
A quarterly utility cost report that someone reads
Monthly tracking against the proforma rate with an alert threshold
Monthly tracking by end use against the rate case we underwrote, with a named person responsible

low.headline: The first real water data you see will be the first bill
low.text: With one building meter you find out after opening, and by then the plumbing is behind finished walls. I would rather see a project spend on submeters now than guess for 20 years about where the money goes.
steps: Add submeters on laundry, kitchen, irrigation and cooling towers
Name the person who reads the water report every month
Set an alert threshold tied to the proforma rate

mid.headline: You have meters. Connect them to the proforma.
mid.text: Submeters pay off when someone compares them against what you underwrote. A quarterly report catches a problem after three months of overpaying. Monthly tracking against the rate case catches it in weeks.
steps: Move water reporting to monthly
Compare cost per room or per unit against the proforma
Track potable and recycled volumes separately once reuse is running

high.headline: You will see a rate increase before it reaches NOI
high.text: Your metering shows what each use costs and which source it comes from. That same data is what a municipality wants to see when you ask about capacity for your next project.
steps: Share recycled-water volumes with the utility
Use the metered data to support LEED v5 water performance credits
Report water numbers to investors next to energy

questions.text: Where is onsite water reuse in this project today?

answers.label: It has not come up
Someone mentioned greywater and it was cut as a green extra
We asked for a water cost savings analysis and it is sitting unread
A greywater recycling or rainwater harvesting system is in the design with a sized treatment room and a payback number
The reuse system is specified, code compliance is confirmed with the local authority, and the savings are in the proforma

questions.text: Where is plumbing design relative to the reuse decision?

answers.label: Plumbing is designed and reuse was never on the table
Plumbing is designed, and adding reuse now means a change order
Plumbing is in schematic design and reuse is still an open question
Reuse is on the agenda before plumbing design starts
Greywater collection, the treatment room and non-potable distribution were set before the plumbing layout was drawn

questions.text: Under the current plan, how much of the building's potable demand could come from recycled greywater or harvested rainwater?

answers.label: We don't know, and nobody has run the numbers
Zero. Everything runs on municipal drinking water.
Under 20%, mainly irrigation from rainwater
20% to 35%, mainly greywater to toilets
35% to 50% or more, with greywater and rainwater combined

low.headline: Reuse is off the table, and your plumbing may lock it out
low.text: Onsite reuse costs the least to add before the plumbing is designed. After that it becomes a change order, and change orders get cut. A commercially certified greywater system can reduce potable demand by about 35% to 50% and reduce sewer discharge by a similar amount. You can't get that from fixtures alone.
steps: Request a water cost savings analysis for this building
Get reuse on the agenda before plumbing design starts
Confirm local code requirements for greywater and rainwater

mid.headline: Reuse is in the conversation. Get it into the drawings.
mid.text: If the savings analysis is still unread, the building is still designed for 100% potable water. What moves it forward is a sized treatment room, a tank location and a payback number the investment committee has seen. The initial CAPEX is small next to what the system saves over 20 years of rising sewer charges.
steps: Reserve a treatment room and tank location in the current plans
Calculate the payback at your utility's published rate
Confirm code compliance with the local authority

high.headline: Your building is designed to use water twice
high.text: Your building will draw less municipal water than it would have, and that frees capacity for the next project in the community. That is worth raising with the municipality early, and it counts toward the LEED v5 Water Reuse credit.
steps: Add rainwater harvesting where greywater alone does not cover demand
Bring the capacity number to the municipality
Plan operator training before commissioning

questions.text: Who on the team is accountable for water and sewer cost after year five?

answers.label: Nobody. The developer plans to sell before it matters.
The future operator, who had no input on the design
The asset manager, who inherits whatever the design delivered
The developer and operator agreed a water cost target during design
One named person owns the 20-year water cost number from design through operations

questions.text: How does this project judge the capital cost of a reuse system?

answers.label: Any water spend above code minimum is cut in value engineering
On first cost alone
On simple payback at today's rates
On payback at the rate increase our utility has published
On 20-year NOI, municipal capacity and LEED v5 Water Reuse credit value together

low.headline: Nobody owns the water bill at year eight
low.text: If the developer plans to sell and the operator inherits the design, the water cost lands on someone who had no say in it. A flat rate in your proforma becomes the next owner's surprise, and a buyer underwriting the building will run the rate you left out.
steps: Name one person who owns the 20-year water cost
Bring the operator into fixture and reuse decisions
Put a water cost target in the design brief

mid.headline: You are judging reuse on today's rates
mid.text: Simple payback at current rates makes a reuse system look slower than it is. On a 200-room hotel the payback is often 4 to 6 years, and every rate increase shortens it. Today's rate is the cheapest one you will pay in the next 20 years.
steps: Recalculate reuse payback at your utility's published increase
Add municipal capacity and LEED v5 credit value to the evaluation
Hold reuse out of value engineering until the 20-year number is on the table

high.headline: You underwrite water the way you underwrite energy
high.text: We routinely protect buildings against rising energy costs. You have done the same for water, and one person owns the result. That makes the building easier to hold and easier to sell.
steps: Revisit the water cost target at every design stage
Hand the 20-year model to the operator at turnover
Use this project as the template for your next build

cta.headline: Want a partner who turns this score into an actual plan?
cta.description: Most people don't fail at the assessment. They fail at sequencing. In 30 minutes I'll show you which two things to fix first, based on your score and your stage. No pitch deck, just the sequencing call.

computed_outputs.label: 20-year water and sewer spend at your utility's rate
Water and sewer cost your proforma leaves out over 20 years
computed_outputs.formula: Math.max(0, (localrate === 0 ? waterbill * 20 : waterbill * (Math.pow(1 + localrate / 100, 20) - 1) / (localrate / 100)) - (proformarate === 0 ? waterbill * 20 : waterbill * (Math.pow(1 + proformarate / 100, 20) - 1) / (proformarate / 100)))

computed_outputs.label: Annual water and sewer bill in year 20 at your utility's rate

Architect or MEP engineer
General contractor
